chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who forgets to say the Takbir during the days of Tashriq. He said: If he forgets until he rises from his place, there is nothing upon him. This does not indicate the negation of obligation regarding what we said, because it only entails the dispensation of re-performance (i'adah) for the one who forgets. And not everything in which re-performance is not obligatory serves as proof that it is not obligatory, because the Friday prayer is obligatory, yet not everyone who forgets it fulfills it with a single Friday prayer; rather, another obligation falls upon him. And there are many similar cases. Likewise, the menstruating woman is not required to make up the prayer, and this does not indicate that the prayer is not obligatory. As for what the report of 'Ammar al-Sabbati included, that it is obligatory after every obligatory and voluntary prayer, the way to handle what relates to the voluntary prayer is to interpret it as a type of preferability (istihbab) rather than obligation and compulsion, which indicates that.

key_terms.أَيَّامِ التَّشْرِيقِ: Days of Tashriq (11th, 12th, 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if one forgets the Takbir during Tashriq days?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the legal status of the Takbir during the Days of Tashriq, distinguishing between the obligation of the act itself and the consequence of forgetting it. He argues that exemption from re-performing the prayer (*i'adah*) does not negate the original obligation, using the analogy of Friday prayer and menstruation to show that non-performance in specific cases does not imply non-obligation. The text further refines the ruling by suggesting that for voluntary prayers, the Takbir may be considered highly recommended (*mustahabb*) rather than strictly obligatory, highlighting the nuanced Shia jurisprudential approach to ritual consistency.
